title: Visiting for Allah
hookLine: a sacred hadith: My love is due to those who visit one another for My sake (Malik)
tomorrow: Dadi says call Hamza. dad says 'he cut me off first.' who's right?

cards: We should hang out soon. Typed, sent, and then, so often, nothing. Here's a visit that actually happens, with a strange detail in the middle.
In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, a man sets out to visit a brother in another town. On the road, God has posted an angel to wait for him. The angel stops him and asks: where are you going?
Why would an angel need to ask?

teach.h: DOES HE OWE YOU A FAVOR?
teach.b: The man answers: to see a brother of mine in that town. The angel presses: does he owe you some favor you're going to collect? No, the man says.
Only that I love him for the sake of God. And the angel tells him: I'm a messenger from God to you, to say that God loves you, as you have loved him for His sake. That's the puzzle solved.
The angel asks the question we all ask: what's in it for you? The test is whether the answer is nothing. A visit with no errand inside it.

Another report, in Malik's Muwatta, is a sacred hadith, God speaking in the Prophet's words: My love is due to those who love one another for My sake, sit together for My sake, visit one another for My sake, and give to one another for My sake.

teach.h: SIT, VISIT, GIVE, FOR MY SAKE.
teach.b: Visit. Give. Ordinary things, done with God as the reason instead of a favor.
And the Prophet's own visits weren't only to fellow Muslims: Sahih al-Bukhari has him going to see a sick Jewish boy who used to serve him.
One to tell a friend tonight: in the hadith, the angel was waiting on the road, not at the door. The going counts.

how: Muslims visit friends and the sick as an act of worship, and may say 'I love you for the sake of God'; the reply from the hadith is 'may He for whose sake you love me love you'.

o: a pilgrimage to the holy sites of Mecca and Medina
going to see someone for God's sake, wanting nothing
visiting a masjid that is not your usual one

games.q: who did what on the road — tap the pairs.
p: sit, visit, give, for My sake
the Prophet went to see him

s: a visit only counts for God if it's to a scholar or a holy place
the man in the hadith was visiting an ordinary brother in another town.
in the hadith, God posts an angel on the road to meet the visitor
and the angel asks whether he's going to collect a favor.
the sacred hadith in Malik names visiting one another for God's sake
alongside loving, sitting together and giving.

games.q: your grandmother's old neighbor moved into a care home across town. she can't do anything for you, and it's a long bus ride. why go?
o: only if it earns you community service hours.
because she's worth the ride; a visit for God's sake needs no return.
a card does the same job and saves the afternoon.
games.why: the angel's question was whether there was a favor to collect. the visit God loves is the one with nothing to collect.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for a minute, across a room or down a hall, as if you were on your way to see someone you love. Feel each step land.
As you walk, bring to mind one person you'd visit with no errand at all, then sit for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Visiting for Allah: going to see someone for God's sake, with no favor to collect. The angel waited on the road.

orig.note: Arabic: 'in God', for God's sake; said of a love or a visit with God as its reason.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: visits for his sake, the kind with no errand inside. Six of ten.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2567 (a man visits a brother in another town; an angel on the road asks if he has a favor to collect; 'God loves you as you loved him for His sake')
Muwatta Malik, Book 51 (Mu'adh ibn Jabal, a sacred hadith: My love is due to those who love, sit together, visit and give to one another for My sake)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1356 (the Prophet visits a sick Jewish boy who used to serve him)
Sunan Abu Dawud 5125 ('I love you for God's sake'; the reply: may He for whose sake you love me love you)
